summary: Red (Mac Plosser and Kevin Rea) never let this nine-hole best-ball turn into a handicapped coin flip, riding Rea’s stroke-leveraged net scoring to a clinical 3&1 win. Even with both Blue players receiving heavy help, the match was effectively decided in the first three holes: Red opened with a net 3 on the par-5 first, then Rea posted a net 2 on the par-3 second and a net 3 on the third to sweep all three. That burst pushed Red to 3 up and sent the win probability screaming from an even start to 59% after one, 77% after two, and 91% after three—about as close to “early doors shut” as match play gets. Blue finally found a foothold on the fourth, where a Blue net 4 beat Red’s net 5 to trim the lead to 2 up, but it was a lone punch. Holes 5 through 7 were a string of halves at net 4s, exactly the kind of stalemate that favors the team already ahead, especially when the trailing side can’t convert their stroke holes into wins. Any hope of a late swing died on the tough par-4 eighth: Rea delivered again with a net 3 to take the hole and restore a 3-up cushion. From there, the ninth was halved at net 3, locking up the 3&1 result. Blue had plenty of strokes on paper; Red simply made sure none of them mattered.

Red’s 1-up win in this nine-hole best ball was a textbook example of surviving an early handicap punch and then squeezing every ounce out of their stroke advantage when it mattered. Blue came out fast thanks largely to Michael Edwards’ heavier allocation of match strokes, turning two straight halves on the card into net wins on holes 1 and 3 and sandwiching William Harris’ clean net par on the par-3 2nd. After three holes, Blue was 3 up and the win probability had already swung into near-lock territory at 90.8% for Blue heading to the 4th—a massive position for such a short match. Then Blue promptly gave the door back. The 4th was the first momentum crack: an ugly collection of 8s from both Blue players allowed Red to steal it with a comparatively “good bad” 6, cutting the deficit to 2. Red kept pressing on the short holes, taking 5 and 7 with net 3s, and suddenly Blue’s cushion was down to 1 despite a Blue response on 6 behind Harris’ net 4. The match flipped on the 8th, the toughest handicap hole, where Red leveraged strokes perfectly—both Quinn and Burgett posted net 3s to win a hole that Blue couldn’t match, erasing the last deficit. All square standing on 9, Burgett delivered the closing blow with a net 4, while Blue’s best ball ballooned to net 6. Blue spent the front half building a lead; Red spent the back half converting strokes into points—and that’s why Red walked off ahead.

Blue’s 4&3 win was built on ruthlessly efficient best-ball scoring and, more importantly, on Red’s inability to cash in the pile of strokes they were getting. With Reid Wesson receiving 14 and Ross Montague 7 (and Brandon Byrd 4), Red had chances to post protected net numbers, but too often their “safe” holes still leaked. Blue jumped in front immediately when Montague produced a net 3 on the opener to beat Red’s best net 4, and they kept pressing on the short par-3 2nd where Red couldn’t turn the hole’s low stroke index into anything useful, losing again with net 5 versus net 4. Even after Red finally landed a counterpunch on 3—Wesson’s net 3 (a stroke well spent) cutting the match back to 1—Blue answered with the decisive stretch: wins on 4, 5, and 6 to balloon the lead to 4 up. That run wasn’t about heroics; it was about Blue repeatedly finding a steady net 3/4 while Red kept handing over net 5s, including another missed opportunity on the par-3 5th and a costly net 5 on 6. The win-probability reflected the squeeze: Blue went from 41.5% at the start to 95.0% by the time they reached the 6th tee. Red did snag 7 to show a flicker, but halved 8 and 9 meant there was no runway left—Blue simply closed the door by not giving holes away.

Plosser and Quinn and the Blue side of Harris and Amagliani played a 9-hole alternate-shot that was so perfectly handicap-neutral it almost felt scripted: nine straight halves on net, and an AS finish that the numbers never really threatened to break. Blue came in receiving nine match strokes relative to Red, and they used that cushion exactly as intended—absorbing Red’s better gross moments without ever letting them translate into a hole on the card. The key story was the repeated pattern where Red “won” the hole in raw scoring but couldn’t win it where it counted. On 12 (the toughest par-4 by stroke index at No. 4), 14 (SI 8), 15 (SI 6), and 18 (SI 2), Red posted 5s while Blue stumbled in with 6s—four clear gross swings—yet every one of them washed out to identical net 5s. That’s alternate shot match play with strokes in a nutshell: Red had to beat Blue by more than one, and they never did. With the match stuck at square the entire way, win probability steadily drifted toward a tie, climbing from roughly 17% after 11 to 40% standing on 18, reflecting how neither side could create separation. Blue didn’t need fireworks; they just needed their strokes to keep cashing, and Red never found the extra gear to make those 6s hurt.

Byrd and Rea turned this alternate-shot nine into a one-way squeeze early, leveraging their two-stroke team edge and never letting Montague and Edwards find a foothold. The match was effectively decided in the opening three holes (10–12), where Red posted three straight net wins on a par 3 and two par 4s, each time simply being one better on the card (4-over-5, 4-over-5, 4-over-5). That clean, mistake-free stretch shoved Red from all square to 3 up in a blink, and the win probability spike told the same story: from an even 41.6% apiece before 10 to 58.9% Red after 10, then 76.5% after 11, and a crushing 90.6% by the time they reached 13. From there, Blue’s problem wasn’t a single blow-up; it was the complete inability to flip a hole back. Holes 13 through 17 were a run of halves with identical net scores, and while that kind of steadiness can stabilize a round, it’s useless when you’re already 3 down—especially in alternate shot, where you need a momentum jolt, not five consecutive stalemates. Red closed the door on 18 by converting their handicap advantage into the only net win of the back-end stretch, taking the hole with a net 4 to Blue’s 5 and sealing the match 3&2. Blue hung around; Red simply banked the early lead and cashed it.

With the teams dead even on handicap strokes, this alternate-shot match was always going to come down to which side could simply keep the ball in play and avoid the big number. John Irvine and Sam Moody did exactly that, blitzing the opening stretch from the start at 10 with four straight hole wins to build a 4-up cushion in a hurry. The scoring pattern tells the story: Blue posted a steady run of net 4s while Ryan Burgett and Reid Wesson kept handing back net 5s on 10 through 13, turning what should have been a tactical grind into a runaway before Red could even settle in. The win probability reflected the early damage—Blue jumped from basically level pre-match to 76.5% after going 2 up, then to 90.6% at 3 up, and by the time they reached 4 up it was effectively in lock territory at 98.1%. Red finally punched back on 14, flipping the script with a clean net 4 to Blue’s 5 to trim it to 3 up, but the response never materialized into a run. From there, the match flatlined: holes 15 through 18 were all halved at net 5, exactly the kind of mutually mediocre stretch that only benefits the team already holding the lead. Blue didn’t need heroics—just competence—and that early four-hole burst was more than enough to close out a 3&2 win.

Even when Wesson made a mess of the par-3 8th (net 8), Byrd’s steady best-ball number kept the hole halved, a perfect snapshot of why this match was decided: Red produced a playable score every hole, while Blue’s “best ball” too often looked like no ball at all.

The problem for Moody is that the scoring detail needed to pinpoint the exact turning holes isn’t in the dataset: hole definitions are missing across the card, and the hole-by-hole score differential feed is blank, so we can’t credibly map the lead changes. What we can say, grounded in the result, is that Wesson consistently won more holes than he gave away, and did it fast—taking four holes of advantage inside six played is the profile of someone cashing net pars and limiting damage while the opponent leaks holes without getting paid back by handicap. Even the lone win-probability snapshot starts dead even, but the deterministic finish tells the real story: Wesson turned a roughly level start into a decisive, early close, and Moody never landed a counterpunch before the match was over.

Plosser didn’t just win—he removed every decision point Harris needed to stage a response.

Byrd did finally show some fight late, beating Montague on 16 and 17 in actual strokes, but Montague’s received strokes neutralized the damage—both holes halved on net, a backbreaking outcome for a player needing a swing. With 18 also halved on net, Montague’s early two-hole blitz stood as the entire difference, and Byrd never found a way to claw any of it back.

Quinn blasted out of the gate with three straight hole wins on 10–12, posting net 3s each time while Irvine leaked net 5s across the same stretch. Irvine actually won it on gross (4 to 5), but Quinn’s stroke neutralized the damage and turned it into a halve at net 4–4, snuffing out Irvine’s best chance to claw back. Irvine never recovered from that opening triple loss, and Quinn never gave him a clean path back.

It was a decent late rally on paper, but it only highlighted the real issue: giving away five holes in a row meant those earned strokes arrived far too late to matter, and the halve on 18 simply closed the door on a match that had already been decided by the opening onslaught.

A halve on 16 kept Louis ahead, and the closing sequence was decisive: Amagliani won 17 with a 5 over 6 to go 2 up, then closed the door on 18 despite both making big numbers, Louis’ 7 beating Rea’s 8. Rea had chances to turn the match with that one-hole surge on 15, but too many loose holes—especially 10 and 18—left him chasing all the way in.

William Harris leaned hard into his seven-shot cushion and turned what could’ve been a tidy nine-hole defense into a handicap clinic, beating Tyler Blocker 2 UP despite giving away nothing early. Blocker actually struck first on the par-3 10th, taking it with a clean net 3 to go 1 UP and briefly push the win probability to 58.3% for Red heading to 11. That edge didn’t last. Harris responded immediately with the round’s loudest punch on 11, carding a 2 to square the match, then took full advantage of where his strokes mattered most: the toughest holes on the card. On the No. 4 handicap 12th, Harris’ net 3 beat Blocker’s 5 to move 1 UP, and when Blocker stumbled again at 14, Harris’ steady net 4 (to Blocker’s 5) extended the lead to 2 UP and effectively flipped the match into Blue control. The win probability reflected it, jumping into “lock territory” at 81.2% for Blue when Harris went 2 UP through five. Blocker’s lone counterpunch came at the par-5 15th with a sharp 3 to win the hole and cut it back to 1, but he couldn’t convert any momentum after that—halving 16 and 17 left him still chasing. Needing something on the stroke-heavy 18th (No. 2 handicap), Blocker instead posted a 5 while Harris used his handicap leverage for a net 3, closing the door with authority.

John Irvine edged Ryan Quinn 1 up in a nine-hole scrap that swung on who better leveraged the handicap math down the stretch. With Irvine receiving three strokes relative to Quinn, the match stayed volatile: Quinn landed the first clean punch back-to-back on holes 12 and 13, turning an early 1-down deficit into a 1-up lead with steady net pars while Irvine leaked a pair of net fives. That two-hole flip was the match’s first real momentum shift, and it showed up in the probabilities too—Blue’s win chances slid from the high-50s early to the low-20s once Quinn went 1 up. Irvine didn’t panic. He halted the bleed with an halve on 14, then squared the match on 15 with a net 4 against Quinn’s net 5, a key response on a hole where Quinn couldn’t afford to give anything away. Quinn briefly looked like he might steal it back with the best swing of the day on the par-3 16th, posting a 2 to regain 1 up, but he couldn’t convert that edge into the clubhouse. Irvine answered immediately on 17 with a winning net 4 to level it again, even as Red’s win probability spiked to 66.7% entering that hole. The deciding moment came on 18: both made 5s, but Irvine’s stroke on the second-handicap hole turned it into a net 4, stealing the hole and the match. Quinn played the golf; Irvine played the format better when it mattered.

Blocker and Mercer walked into this 9-hole two-man scramble giving nothing away on strokes, while Harris and Irvine had to chase from one back on the card but with a single match stroke in their pocket, and it showed in the way the match swung on just a handful of moments. Red landed the first punch on 1 with a clean net 4 to Blue’s 5, only to hand it straight back on 2 when Blue answered with a net 4 to Red’s 5. After a halve on the par-5 3rd, Red grabbed what looked like a foothold on the par-3 4th, beating Blue 3 to 4 to go 1 up, and then proceeded to sit on it for three straight halves (5 through 7). That conservative stretch was efficient—Blue couldn’t flip a single hole—but it also left the door cracked. The win-probability model reflected that squeeze: with Red 1 up and only a few holes left, Blue’s win chances dipped into single digits by the 8th, essentially screaming “last call.” Blue finally kicked it in on 8 with the round’s sharpest swing, a net 3 to Red’s 4 to square the match. Then the handicap pressure hit on the toughest hole: both teams made actual 4s on 9, but Blue’s match stroke turned it into a net 3 and a hole win. That late steal didn’t change the official result—this one finished tied—but it underlined the difference: Red played steadier, Blue leveraged the one stroke exactly when it mattered.

Luke Jensen and Hunter Meriwether edged Mac Plosser and Kyle Cummins 1 UP in a nine-hole two-man scramble that was as tight as the scoreline suggests, with the handicap structure quietly steering the finish. Red entered as the lower-handicap side (0 strokes relative), and they used that advantage early by striking first on No. 1 with a clean net 3 to go 1 up. But every time Red threatened to separate, Blue answered immediately: Blue squared the match on the difficult No. 2 (handicap 5) with a net 4 to Red’s net 5, then Red bounced right back on the par-5 third, winning it outright after Blue leaked to a net 6. That back-and-forth tug was reflected in the win probabilities, which swung sharply whenever a team grabbed a one-hole edge—Red’s chances spiking above 59% twice when they went 1 up—yet neither side could hold momentum for more than a hole. The middle of the round turned into a trench fight. No. 4 flipped again with Blue’s net 3 on the par 3, and from there the match stalled into a run of halves on 5, 7, and 8, plus a crucial stalemate on No. 6 where Blue’s extra strokes turned an actual-loss 5 into a net halve at 4—exactly the kind of handicap leverage that keeps a match alive. All square heading to the hardest hole on the card, Blue finally cashed: both teams made actual 3s on No. 9, but Blue’s stroke converted it into a net 2, stealing the hole and the match in one clean, clinical finish.

Blue (Drew Hursey/Ross Montague) scraped out a 1 UP win in a 9-hole scramble that swung wildly despite Red (Brandon Byrd/Jay Edwards) carrying the better team handicap and giving up two strokes on paper. Early, Blue played like the side that was supposed to be getting help, taking the first two holes with clean net 4s while Red stumbled to back-to-back 5s. That 2-up jump drove Blue’s win probability to 77.2% after the second, and it looked like they might put it away quickly. Red didn’t fold, though, and their response was sharp and immediate. They clawed one back on the par-5 third, then detonated the match on the par-3 fourth with a net 2 to Blue’s 4, wiping out the deficit in two holes. After a halve at five, Red seized full control on the toughest par-4 of the side (hole 6, stroke index 3), posting a net 4 while Blue leaked a 6. That single swing flipped the match and pushed Red’s win probability into command territory (64.5% with Red 1 up). But Red couldn’t cash in from there. A routine halve on seven kept them ahead, then Blue punched back on the par-3 eighth with a net 3 to square it. On the closing hole—stroke index 1—Blue found the one place their handicap edge actually mattered, turning a solid 4 into a net 3 while Red slumped to a 6. In a match decided by margins, Red’s late failure to protect the hardest hole was the difference.

Wynn and Amagliani took a 2&1 decision for Blue in a nine-hole scramble that was tighter on paper than the match-play scoreline suggests, mainly because Red started with the handicap edge but couldn’t turn it into enough net wins. With Red receiving no match strokes to Blue’s two, the pressure was on Wesson and Rea to simply be steadier—and the first two holes delivered nothing but traded punches, matching 6s and staying all square. The first real separation came on the par-5 third, where Blue posted a sharp 4 to Red’s 6 and jumped in front; win probability immediately swung from an even split to Blue controlling the match (60.5% by the next tee) and it never fully relaxed after that. Red’s best response was exactly where you’d expect it: on the hardest par-4 sixth (stroke index 3), they found a clean 4 while Blue leaked a 5 to square the match again. That was the turning point opportunity, but Red couldn’t build on it. Blue answered with the decisive two-hole burst on 7 and 8, taking both with 5 over 7 and then 4 over 5 to move 2 up, the kind of mini-run that effectively ended it—reflected in the win probability spike to 67.4% after 7 and near lock territory after 8. Red did at least salvage pride on 9 by beating Blue’s 6 with a 5, but Blue’s net 5 (using their strokes) halved the hole and closed the door. The difference was simple: Blue won three holes outright, and when Red finally won one, they couldn’t prevent the immediate counterpunch.

With the teams playing off level weighted handicaps, this nine-hole modified alternate shot was a straight net shootout, and Blocker/Edwards simply made fewer mistakes when it mattered. Red struck first on 10 by taking par net against Blue’s net bogey to go 1 up, a clean early punch that immediately pushed their win probability near 59% after 11. Blue answered with their best swing of the match on the toughest early test, stealing the 12th when Red leaked to a net 6 against Blue’s net 5, snapping the match back to all square and resetting the win probabilities to an even 39.8% apiece heading to 13. From there, the match turned into a grind: three straight halves on 13–14–17 and another on 18, with neither side able to manufacture separation through the closing stretch. The difference was that Red found two scoring edges on the softer handicap holes and cashed them in. On 15 Red again posted net par while Blue stumbled to net bogey, and the very next hole, 16, Red repeated the formula—net 5 to Blue’s net 6—to extend the lead to 2 up. That two-hole burst was decisive not just on the card but in leverage: Blue’s win chances collapsed to 13.5% before 16, and by 17 Red had the match effectively locked (91% to win). Blue halved the last two but never recovered from consecutive bogeys in alternate shot, and Red closed out 2&1 without giving anything back.

Mac Plosser and Kyle Cummins never let this nine-hole alternate-shot turn into a handicap scrap; they controlled it early and then squeezed the life out of the back side to secure a 2&1 win over John Irvine and Ross Montague. Even with Blue receiving two match strokes, Red’s cleaner net golf on the opening stretch created separation before the match had any chance to settle. Red struck first on 10 when Blue opened with a costly net 6, and they doubled down on the key swing hole at 12 (stroke index 4) by posting a net 5 to Blue’s net 6. That one-two punch pushed Red to 2 up through three and, more importantly, shoved the win probability firmly into Red’s hands—jumping from a coin flip at the start to nearly 80% by the time they walked off 13 still 2 up. From there it was classic alternate-shot match management: five straight halves from 13 through 17, with neither side finding a way to manufacture a stolen hole or leverage Blue’s strokes into momentum. By 17, the numbers called it practically over, with Blue’s win probability hitting 0% and Red sitting at 91% to close. Blue finally cashed a stroke at 18 with a net 3 to win the hole, but it only trimmed the margin to 1 down with no holes left to play—too little, too late, and never a real threat after Red’s early burst.

Blue’s 2&1 win over Mercer/Rea was built on exactly what alternate shot punishes: one messy stretch that your opponents actually convert. On paper Red had the handicap edge (they played off 0 match strokes to Blue’s 2), but Meriwether/Amagliani still won the net battle early by simply keeping big numbers off the card when it mattered. After trading the opening two holes on the back nine, Blue flipped the match on the hardest par-4 in the set (12, stroke index 4) with a clean net 4 against Red’s net 6 to go 1 up, then immediately pressed that advantage on 13 and 14 to run the lead to 3 up through five holes. That three-hole surge was the decisive stretch: Red didn’t just lose holes, they leaked shots in bunches (net 6 on the par-3 13 and net 7 on the par-5 14), and in alternate shot you don’t get a second chance to “have the other guy bail you out.” The win probability reflected the squeeze—Blue jumped from essentially a coin flip at all square to 80.4% at 2 up, then hit near lock territory at 94.9% when they reached 3 up. Red finally stopped the bleeding with a win on 15 and clawed one more back in gross terms on 18, but Blue’s two-stroke handicap safety net turned that last push into a net halve. With 16 and 17 also halved, Blue never had to do anything heroic late—just close the door.

Brandon Byrd and Reid Wesson had to give Drew Hursey and Daniel Wynn five shots in this nine-hole modified alternate-shot, and it showed early as Blue took the opener at 10 with a clean net 4 to Red’s 6 to grab a 1-up lead. Red answered immediately on the par-3 11, but the real handicap leverage came at 12, the toughest of the side: Blue’s 5 became a net 4, flipping what could’ve been a half into a win and pushing them back in front. When Blue then outright won 13 with a sharp net 3 to Red’s 5, they stretched it to 2-up and briefly had the match in a stranglehold—win probability spiked to 80.4% for Blue heading into 14. Red’s response was the defining stretch. They finally steadied the alternating rhythm and took 14 and 15 back-to-back, erasing the deficit without needing any net help—just cleaner execution while Blue leaked shots. Just as the match reset to all square, both sides traded big numbers on the par-5 16, and Blue’s net 7 edged Red’s 8 to move 1-up again. Then Blue handed it right back on 17 with an ugly net 8, gifting Red the hole and returning the match to dormie-all-square with one to play. On 18, Red’s one-shot actual advantage wasn’t enough to beat Blue’s stroke on the No. 2 handicap hole, and the net 5s produced a fitting halve and a tie overall.

Blue’s John Irvine and Hunter Meriwether earned a clinical 2&1 best-ball win over Brandon Byrd and Kevin Rea by doing the simple match-play thing Red never managed: turn Red’s heavy stroke package into actual hole control. With Irvine playing off scratch in the match and Meriwether receiving 10, Blue’s floor was steady all nine, while Red’s best chances largely depended on Rea converting his 18 strokes into net birdies and stress-free pars. Blue struck first on the opening par 5, where Meriwether’s net 4 beat Red’s net 6 to grab the early lead. Red briefly leveraged the handicap on the par-3 second as Rea posted a net 3 to square the match, but that was more a spark than a shift. Irvine answered immediately on the third with a net 4 to win, and even when Blue couldn’t separate on four (all square at net 4), they kept piling on pressure. The match was effectively decided in the 5–6 stretch. Irvine’s net 3 on the par 3 at five pushed Blue to 2 up, and then both Blue players produced net 5s on six while Red stumbled to a net 6, inflating the margin to 3 up and blasting Blue’s win probability into the mid-90s by the next hole. Red finally punched back on seven with Rea’s net 2, but it was too late; an actual win on eight only halved, and a net halved nine closed it out with Blue never giving the match back within one after the third.

Blue’s 3&2 best-ball win was a clean example of how to weaponize strokes, even against a side anchored by the low man. Mac Plosser (5) and Jay Edwards (15) actually landed the first punch when Plosser’s 4 on the opener gave Red a quick 1-up lead, and Red’s win probability jumped to 59% heading to the third. But from there, Daniel Wynn (22) took over the net side of the card and never let Red breathe. The swing started on the stroke holes where Blue’s extra shots mattered most. Wynn’s net 4 on No. 3 flipped a previously halved hole into a Blue win, erasing Red’s early edge. Then the match turned vicious on No. 4: Red posted ugly sevens while Wynn produced a tidy net 3, a two-shot net gap that felt like a knockout in nine-hole match play. In the span of two holes, the match went from Red controlling the script to all square and then Blue 1-up. Blue kept pressing on the short par 3s, stealing No. 5 and No. 7 on net with Wynn’s back-to-back net 3 and net 2, stretching the lead to 3-up. Win probability reflected the rout: Blue surged to 61% after No. 5 and was deep in lock territory (83%–87%) by Nos. 6–7. Red did manage actual-score wins on Nos. 8 and 9, but they couldn’t convert them into holes because Blue’s strokes turned both into halves. That was the match in a sentence: Blue cashed handicap where it counted, and Red’s late “wins” didn’t move the needle.

Blue’s 4&3 win was basically a case study in how to weaponize handicap strokes in best ball, and Red never found a counterpunch. Even with Tyler Blocker sitting at the low end of the match handicap ladder, Drew Hursey and Ross Montague had so many shots in play that “pars” turned into automatic net birdies. The opening stretch told the whole story: holes 1 through 4 were all halved in gross scoring, but Blue won every one on net, moving to 4 up without Red really making a mistake—just getting quietly out-leveraged. That’s the brutal math of best ball when both Blue players are turning the same number into a lower net. The win probability tracked that suffocation, jumping from an even start to 59.0% after the first hole, then ballooning to 90.8% by the time Blue went 3 up, and essentially into lock territory at 98.2% when they reached 4 up after four. Red finally produced a spark on the par-3 5th, where Kyle Cummins posted a clean 2 to steal one back, trimming it to 3 down and briefly making the match feel human again. But any comeback hopes died immediately on 6, where Montague delivered a 4 that played as a net 3 to flip the hole, restoring a 4-up cushion. From there, Blue kept stacking net edges—again with gross ties—closing the door with net wins on 7, 8, and 9. Red simply couldn’t convert their opportunities into net wins often enough, and Blue never let the handicap strokes go to waste.

Blue’s William Harris and Luke Jensen closed out a 2 UP best-ball win over Owen Mercer and Reid Wesson by doing the simple match-play math: they didn’t need heroics, just fewer wasted holes against a Red side getting plenty of strokes (Mercer 10, Wesson 13) but rarely cashing them. The first three holes told the story of the day—Blue won two of them on gross (1 and 3), yet Red’s handicap help kept the match square on net. Even that couldn’t keep the door shut for long. Red finally landed a clean net punch on the 4th when Mercer’s net 3 flipped the match to 1 up, and the win probability reflected it—Red jumped to 61.2% heading to the 5th. That advantage lasted exactly one hole. Blue answered immediately on the par-3 5th with matching net 3s from Harris and Jensen to level, then decisively took control on the 6th when Red posted a messy net 5 against Blue’s net 4. From there, Blue managed the finish like a team that understood best ball: the 7th and 8th were halved on net despite Blue winning the 7th on gross, keeping Red from leveraging strokes to create late pressure. The match was effectively decided on the closing par-5 9th (stroke index 1). With Red still only 1 down, Blue slammed the door—Harris’s 4 and Jensen’s net 4 beat Mercer’s net 5, stretching it to 2 up and ending it. Blue’s win probability surged into lock territory after taking the lead on 6 and never dipped again.

Jay Edwards stole a 1 UP win over Drew Hursey in a nine-hole singles match that looked dead and buried for Red after a brutal early stretch. With Hursey receiving the lone handicap stroke in the match, Edwards couldn’t afford waste, but he handed Blue momentum anyway: a dropped hole at the par-4 11th (6 to 5) was followed by a decisive loss at the par-4 12th where Hursey posted the round’s cleanest number with a 4 to Edwards’ 6. When Hursey tacked on another at the 14th (4 to 5), Blue was 3 UP through five and firmly in control; the win probabilities reflected it, peaking at 93.6% for Blue heading to the 15th, essentially “lock” territory in a nine-hole sprint. Then Hursey opened the door—and Edwards sprinted through it. The par-5 15th flipped the match’s energy in one swing as Hursey ballooned to an 8 against Edwards’ steady 5, cutting the deficit to 2. Edwards kept pressing with no letup, winning three straight: a sharp 3 on the par-3 16th (to Hursey’s 5), then surviving ugly golf on 17 with a 7 that still beat Hursey’s 8, and finally closing with another gritty win at 18 (7 to 8). In the end, Edwards didn’t win by being flawless; he won by cashing in hard when Hursey’s mistakes arrived, turning a 3-down hole into a four-hole closing knockout.

Ross Montague edged Owen Mercer 1 UP in a nine-hole singles that swung hard on a couple of Mercer mistakes, then nearly flipped back the other way before Ross slammed the door. With just one stroke separating their course handicaps, there wasn’t much built-in cushion either way, and the early holes showed it: the match opened with two straight halves on 10 and 11, dead even on both gross and net. The first real crack came at 12 (stroke index 4), where Mercer posted a net 6 and handed Montague the hole with a steadier net 5. Mercer didn’t stop the bleeding on 14 (SI 8) either, again losing with a net 6 to Montague’s net 5, and suddenly Blue was 2 UP with momentum and an 81.2% win probability after 14—borderline cruise control. Then Montague made it interesting. A costly net 7 on the par-5 15 let Mercer claw one back, and Mercer kept pressing, leveling the match with a clean net 3 on the short par-3 16 when Montague slipped to a net 4. From there it became a two-hole sprint. Montague’s best moment was perfectly timed: a net 3 on 17 to win the hole and jump back in front. Mercer needed something on 18 (SI 2) but could only halve it at net 5, and Montague’s steadiness when it mattered most preserved the narrow win.

Hunter Meriwether edged Kyle Cummins 1 up in a nine-hole singles that swung back and forth until Blue’s handicap advantage finally mattered on the last green. With Meriwether receiving two strokes relative to Cummins, the match was always going to be about whether Blue could survive the volatility and then cash in when the stroke holes arrived—and that’s exactly how it played out. Blue struck first on the par-3 10th as Cummins opened with a costly 6, but Cummins answered immediately at 11 to square it, and the early pattern was set: one player would land a punch, the other would return it. Meriwether reclaimed the lead at the tough 12th when Cummins slipped to a 7, only for Cummins to level again at 13 and then take his first lead at 14 with a steady 4 against Meriwether’s 6. At that point the win probabilities reflected real Red control, peaking with Cummins 1 up and Red favored (61.6%) heading to 15. But Cummins couldn’t protect that edge. Meriwether flipped 15 with a clean 5 against another Red blow-up 7, and although Cummins briefly surged again by winning the par-3 16th with a sharp 2, the late mistakes returned at the worst time. Cummins’ 7 on 17 handed momentum back, and on the stroke-index-2 finisher Meriwether’s net 3 (4 with the stroke) beat Cummins’ 5 to steal the match on 18.

William Harris took full advantage of his four-shot cushion and never let Tyler Blocker get comfortable, closing out a tidy 2&1 win over the nine-hole run from 10 to 18. After a routine halve on the par-3 10th, Blocker blinked first on 11, posting a 5 to Harris’s 4, and Blue was immediately 1 up. The key pattern of the match showed up early: when Blocker did find a response, he couldn’t make it count on the card. On 12, Blocker’s 4 beat Harris’s 5 in gross terms, but Harris’s handicap stroke on that hole turned it into a net halve, snuffing out what should have been Red’s momentum swing and keeping Blue’s advantage intact. From there, Harris tightened the screws with steadiness and one timely punch. Holes 13, 15, 16, and 17 were all halved with matching scores, exactly the kind of low-drama golf that plays up when you’re the player receiving strokes. The decisive moment came on 14 when Harris turned a solid par-3 on the par-4 into a clean win over Blocker’s 4, stretching the lead to 2 up and pushing Blue’s win probability into “near-lock” territory—over 80% by the time they reached 15. Blocker needed something special coming home and didn’t get it. On the 18th, Harris slammed the door with a 4 that became a net 3 thanks to another stroke, while Blocker stumbled to a 5, ending it with room to spare.

Luke Jensen never had to worry about handicap math in this one because there wasn’t any—both players played off level course handicaps with zero strokes, and Jensen simply delivered the cleaner nine to close out a 3&2 win. The tone was set immediately on the par-3 10th when Jensen opened with a net 3 to grab the early 1-up lead, and then Brandon Byrd handed over real separation on 11 with a brutal net 7 against Jensen’s steady net 4. That swing pushed Jensen to 2-up and spiked his win probability from a coin flip at the start to 75.1% by the time they reached 12. Byrd briefly stabilized with a halve on the tougher handicap-4 12th, but he couldn’t stop the bleeding on 13, losing again with a net 6 to Jensen’s 5 as Jensen stretched it to 3-up. Byrd finally landed a punch on 14, winning with a net 5 when Jensen slipped to a 6, and for a moment the match had a pulse again at 2-down—yet even that came with Jensen still sitting at a commanding 91.1% to win. The decisive answer arrived on the par-5 15th: Byrd posted another net 7, Jensen a net 5, and the lead ballooned back to 3-up with three to play. A routine halve on 16 kept the door shut, and Jensen slammed it on 17 with a net 4 to Byrd’s 5 to finish it early. Jensen didn’t need heroics—he just avoided the big numbers Byrd couldn’t.

John Irvine squeezed out a 1 UP singles win over Mac Plosser, and he did it the smart way: by turning his four-stroke cushion into immediate net pressure on the toughest places to give shots. After both opened with steady net pars on 10, Plosser’s blow-up 6 on 11 handed Irvine the first lead, and the match’s shape was basically set. The real dagger came one hole later on the stroke-index 4 par 4, where matching 4s on the card still meant Irvine’s net 3 took the hole. Two up through three holes, Irvine didn’t need fireworks; he needed Plosser to keep failing to punish the spots where Irvine wasn’t getting help. From 13 through 16 the match went into a grind of halves—four straight—all square on both actual and net scoring, which suited the player already dormie-adjacent. The win probability reflected that slow squeeze: once Irvine hit 2 UP, his chances climbed from 58.9% after 12 to 85.0% by 16, essentially lock territory without him having to win another hole. Plosser finally showed some late-life on 17, flipping the script with a clean 4 against Irvine’s 6 to cut it to 1 UP, and he even won 18 on the card (4 to 5). But 18 was stroke index 2—exactly where Irvine’s handicap advantage mattered most—so his extra shot turned that 5 into a net 4 and halved the hole. Plosser’s late rally was real; it just ran straight into the math.

Daniel Wynn leaned hard into his four-stroke edge and turned what started as a dead-even nine-hole set into a clinical 4&2 win for Blue, mostly by winning the holes where handicap leverage actually mattered. After both players opened with matching net 4s on 10, Reid Wesson briefly looked comfortable when Wynn stumbled to an ugly net 8 on 11, handing Red a 1-up lead and pushing the win probability toward Wesson (58.9% after 11). That was as good as it got. The match flipped immediately on 12, the toughest handicap hole in the stretch, where Wynn’s stroke did real damage: a net 4 against Wesson’s net 6 not only erased the deficit but snapped the momentum back to square. From there Wynn stacked pressure with a three-hole burst on 13–15, winning each on net and turning a tie into 3-up in short order. Wesson’s scores (net 7 on 13 and net 6 on 14–15) simply couldn’t keep pace, while Wynn mixed in just enough stability—and one standout par-5 performance—to make the extra shots count. By the time Wynn took 16 as well (net 3 to net 5), Blue was 4-up and the win probability effectively hit lock territory at 96.1%. Wesson did show some late fight by taking 17 and forcing a net halve on 18, but those were consolation points. The match was decided when Wynn stopped wasting his strokes and Wesson failed to capitalize on the holes where Wynn was most vulnerable.

Louis Amagliani edged Kevin Rea 1 up in a nine-hole scrap that swung on big numbers and even bigger missed chances to cash in on the handicap. With Rea receiving a single stroke for the match, the net scoring still played essentially straight up—and that put a premium on simply avoiding disasters. Amagliani set the tone immediately by taking the par-3 10th with a tidy 3 against Rea’s 5, but Rea answered on 11 when Amagliani handed over the hole with a 6. The match’s first real turning point came on the stroke-index 4 twelfth: Rea’s 8 was a complete hole-killer, and Amagliani’s 4 flipped it right back to Blue, a swing that mattered because it came on one of the tougher holes where you can’t afford to leak shots. From there it was a tug-of-war. Rea steadied himself by winning 13, but Amagliani punched back on 14 and then created separation on the par-5 15th, taking it 6 to 8 to go 2 up. Win probability reflected that squeeze—Blue jumped into near-lock territory at 85% heading to 16. Rea wasn’t done, grabbing 16 and 17 to erase the deficit and square the match, but after all that work he left himself exposed on the hardest hole coming in. On 18, Rea’s 8 against Amagliani’s 7 was the final giveaway, and Blue took the match with the cleaner finish.

Tyler Blocker and Owen Mercer delivered a textbook nine-hole scramble, beating Daniel Wynn and Louis Amagliani 3 & 2 by doing what low-stroke teams must do: win the holes where the other side can’t actually cash in its handicap edge. Blue came in with a massive 10-shot allowance relative to Red, and they did use it—netting wins on three of the tougher indexes (they took the par-4 third, plus the No. 1 handicap eighth, and then ninth). The problem was that those strokes only mattered after Red had already built a cushion with clean, mistake-free scoring on the holes Blue couldn’t afford to leak. The first real swing came immediately. Red won the opener outright, then on the par-5 second they still halved despite Blue’s net stroke turning a 6 into a 5—an early missed opportunity that kept Red in front. Blue briefly flipped momentum on the No. 3 handicap hole at the third, where their net 4 beat Red’s 5 to square the match, but that was as good as it got. Red answered with the decisive stretch: a dominant win at the par-3 fourth (3 to 5), then back-to-back wins at five and six to push the match to 3 up. That run shoved Red’s win probability into near-lock territory, jumping from roughly 61% after five to 84% after six and 98% after seven. Blue’s late net rally on eight and nine only trimmed the margin; it never threatened the result because Red had already banked too many holes while Blue was busy “winning” strokes instead of holes.

With both scrambles set at level terms on strokes, this nine-hole set turned into a clean, net-for-net shootout where every mistake actually mattered. Kyle Cummins and Kevin Rea leaned on a two-stroke edge in the scramble handicap, but for most of the nine it was Drew Hursey and Hunter Meriwether who played like the side giving shots. Both teams made 5, but Red’s handicap finally mattered—turning that into a net win (4 versus 5) and dragging the match back to 1-down after Blue had briefly reached 91.9% win territory. All square still looked unlikely, but Red finished with their best sequence: a net win on 9 (Red 4, Blue 6) completed a late two-hole surge to steal the halve. Blocker and Mercer walked into this nine-hole modified alternate-shot giving away six strokes to Harris and Wynn, and still managed to make the handicap math feel irrelevant. Meriwether and Amagliani took a match that was supposed to be tight on paper—Blue giving four strokes in a nine-hole alternate-shot sprint—and turned it into a controlled 3&1 win by simply refusing to waste holes. Red (Mallory/Rea) came in giving away nothing on paper—actually getting a hefty 10-shot cushion in this nine-hole modified alternate shot—and they needed every bit of it to survive Blue’s (Montague/Hursey) steadier baseline golf. Blue controlled most of the round, but Red’s late conversion of strokes flipped what should’ve been a routine closeout into a halved match.

Quinn and Mercer came in giving away nothing on paper but receiving five shots as a side, and for a while it looked like they’d actually make that handicap edge matter. They dug an early hole with a messy 6 on the opener (10) to lose immediately, then answered with their best piece of net strategy on the hardest stretch: on the stroke-index 4 par 4 (12) they turned matching fives into a net win, using their strokes exactly the way an underdog pair has to in alternate shot. The finish flipped anyway, and it flipped fast. On 16, Blue’s 7 opened the door and Red walked through, then Quinn/Mercer backed it up with a straight-up 4 over Blue’s 5 on 17 to erase the deficit entirely. All square on 18, Blue finally steadied with the better gross score (4 to 5), but Red’s stroke on the index-2 finisher turned that into a halve, sealing a tie that felt like Blue let get away.

Red never let this best-ball match breathe, riding handicap leverage and timely low balls to a clinical 3&2. From there, Red slammed the door at the pivotal seventh, where Mercer’s actual 4 became a net 3 and Blue stumbled home with 5 and 6—pushing the match to 3 up and 86.7% Red. Halves at 8 and 9 were enough; Blue’s problem wasn’t effort late, it was wasting their best holes by failing to beat Red’s net ball.

Red (Jay Edwards and Kevin Rea) squeezed out a 1-up best-ball win over Drew Hursey and Hunter Meriwether in a match that never stopped seesawing, with handicap leverage ultimately tipping the ninth. Blue kept it alive with a birdie-like 3 on the par-3 8th, but the match was decided on the hardest hole: Rea’s clutch net 3 on the 9th (off his strokes) punished Blue’s 5s and sealed it.

Red’s Neely Mallory and Kyle Cummins leveraged their hefty stroke advantage exactly the way a best-ball team is supposed to, beating Luke Jensen and Ross Montague 2&1 in a match that was effectively decided by ruthless conversion on the holes where net pars become birdies. After an opening halve, Red struck first on the par-5 2nd when Mallory’s steady net 5 beat a Blue 6, only for Blue to answer immediately at the par-3 3rd with matching 3s from Jensen and Montague to square it. That was as close as it stayed for long. When Montague finally pulled one back on the 6th with a clean net 5 on the par 5, it briefly cut the lead to one and lifted Blue’s chances off the mat—but Red slammed the door on the 7th, again turning matching actual 4s into net 3s to restore a two-up cushion. Blue’s 2&1 win was a clean example of handicap leverage beating raw scoring, with Daniel Wynn and Louis Amagliani turning a strokes-heavy setup into a steady drip of net birdies that Red never fully answered. Red finally cashed in on 7, where Byrd produced a key net 3 to win and cut it to 2 down, but the damage was already done. Halves at 8 and a net stalemate on the difficult 9 meant Blue never gave the door back, closing exactly when they needed to.

John Irvine’s 2 UP win over Ryan Quinn was a nine-hole clinic in turning early advantage into match-play suffocation, especially with Quinn receiving two strokes and still never finding a spot to cash them in. After another half on 17, Quinn reached 18 needing something, but Irvine slammed the door with the round’s cleanest finish: a net 4 against Quinn’s net 5 to finally stretch it to 2 UP. In a match this tight, Quinn’s problem wasn’t one big blow-up; it was never taking a hole back after losing the first.

Owen Mercer and Drew Hursey split the points in a wild nine-hole singles that looked finished early, then got flipped twice by sheer volatility. Ross Montague’s 2&1 win over Jay Edwards was essentially decided before Edwards ever got a chance to leverage his two-shot handicap cushion. Kyle Cummins took a 2&1 singles point for Red with a sharp nine-hole reversal that punished every opening Daniel Wynn left on the table, even with Wynn receiving two strokes on the card. Brandon Byrd took full control of this nine-hole singles from the start and never really let Luke Jensen breathe, converting his four-shot handicap edge into a clinically managed 3&2 win for Red. Neely Mallory turned this nine-hole singles match into a clinic in pressure conversion, using a two-stroke handicap edge to build separation early and never really letting Hunter Meriwether breathe. Even when Mallory blinked on the drivable-ish par-4 14th (net 5 to Meriwether’s net 4), the response was sharp: a win on 15 restored the two-hole cushion, and then the decisive blow landed on the toughest handicap hole, 16. Meriwether did manage late cosmetic damage with wins on 17 and 18, but that only narrowed the margin on paper; the match had already been decided by the 11–12 burst and Mallory’s perfect use of strokes on 16.

Kevin Rea and Louis Amagliani finished deadlocked in a nine-hole singles that swung hard in both directions despite identical course handicaps, meaning every hole was a straight net fight with no stroke safety net. Brandon Byrd and Jay Edwards (Red), giving away three match strokes to Drew Hursey and Daniel Wynn (Blue) under the weighted scramble handicap, still controlled the nine in a tidy 2&1 win. With the team handicaps dead even, Plosser/Mercer and Irvine/Montague played a straight-up nine-hole scramble where every swing mattered, and it ended fittingly all square. Daniel Wynn and Louis Amagliani took a tight nine-hole scramble and turned it into a controlled 3&1 win by squeezing maximum value out of the four strokes they received against Ryan Quinn and Kevin Rea. A routine halve on 9 finished it, with Red simply unable to convert their low-handicap advantage into net separation when it mattered most.

With the teams dead even on handicap strokes, this alternate-shot nine turned into a straight-up execution test, and Edwards/Mallory made it brutally simple: win early, then suffocate. With the teams dead even on strokes (both sides carrying the same weighted team handicap and getting no net help), this nine-hole modified alternate shot from 10 to 18 turned into a straight-up scrap where every swing had to be earned. Montague and Amagliani’s 2&1 win was a classic nine-hole alternate-shot flip: weather the early punches, then slam the door with a ruthless four-hole run that Red never matched. Quinn and Mercer took control early in this alternate-shot sprint and never really let Irvine and Hursey get comfortable, closing out a 2&1 win with both sides playing off scratch in the match (no strokes given). Red’s 1 UP best-ball win was a classic nine-hole grind where the handicap leverage finally showed up just in time to erase an early Blue blitz.
